files.lesson.md: --- order: 6 unit: expressions node: AC9M7A02 n3 title: An expression for any case summary: Say what the letter stands for, write an expression for the situation, then test it with a number you can check. One expression then gives the answer for every case. language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A party for 5 people, 50 people or 500: one expression gives the cost for all of them, if you say clearly what the letter stands for." connection: fence-posts # data/connections/maths.yml (documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8147 url: http://127.0.0.1:8147/index.html readySelector: "#sl-g" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: formula.yml#pic, caption: "Let $g$ be the number of guests. A hall costs 60 dollars plus 5 dollars per guest: $C = 5g + 60$. With 10 guests: $5 \\times 10 + 60 = 110$ dollars." } explainClip: query: { code: "@formula.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Say what the letter stands for, then write the expression" say: "Say what the letter stands for, then write the expression." clip: - caption: { text: "A hall: 60 dollars, plus 5 dollars for each guest.", say: "A hall costs sixty dollars, plus five dollars for each guest." } - caption: { text: "Let g be the number of guests.", say: "Let g stand for the number of guests." } - caption: { text: "g guests cost 5g. Add the hire: C = 5g + 60.", say: "g guests cost five g. Add the hire: five g plus sixty." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Test it: 10 guests cost 50 + 60 = 110 dollars.", say: "Test it: ten guests cost fifty plus sixty: one hundred and ten." } - click: Make g bigger - caption: { text: "The same expression gives any number of guests.", say: "The same expression gives the cost for any number of guests." } - expect: { selector: ".rulework", contains: "C = 5 × 20 + 60 = 160 dollars" } - wait: 1200 --- So far each expression was written from one sentence about a number. A real situation has parts: a fee, a price for each one, a number of people. To write one expression for all of it, first say **what the letter stands for**, then build the expression, then **test** it with a case you can check in words. After that one expression gives the answer for any number. ## Predict: what should the letter be? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to what the letter stands for exposes letting it stand for the thing that is being worked out, instead of the quantity that changes." check: type: predict q: "A school trip costs 12 dollars per student plus a 50 dollar bus. You want one expression for the total cost. What should the letter stand for?" options: ["The number of students", "The total cost", "The 12 dollars", "The bus"] actual: "The number of students. It is the quantity that changes from trip to trip. The cost is worked out from it (12n + 50), and 12 and 50 are constants." ``` If $n$ is the number of students, what does 1 student cost? What do 10 cost? ## Run: one expression, many trips ```step stage: run insight: "Moving n and reading off the cost shows that one expression gives every case, and the parts mean what the story says." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#run", height: 420 } check: { type: board, text: "$n$ is the number of students on the trip. How much does a trip of 20 students cost?", when: "n = 20" } ``` The rule is $C = 12n + 50$. Set $n$ to 0: what does the 50 mean? What does the 12 mean? Was your prediction right? ## Investigate: from a situation to an expression ```step stage: investigate insight: "Name the letter, write what changes, add what is paid once, then test with one case; the letter stands for a number, not for the objects." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A phone plan costs 15 dollars a month plus 4 dollars per GB. Let $g$ be the number of GB used. Write an expression for the monthly cost." answer: "4g + 15" feedback: - ["15g + 4", "The 15 dollars is paid once, whatever you use. Which amount is multiplied by g?"] - ["19g", "Don't combine them. The 15 is paid once; only the 4 is paid for each GB."] explain: "4g + 15: 4 dollars for each of g GB, plus 15 dollars once." - check: type: question q: "Zoe starts with \"Let $n$ be the cost\" for tickets that cost 9 dollars each. Why is that not a good start?" options: - "The cost changes with the number of tickets, so the letter should stand for the number of tickets" - "A letter can never stand for a cost" - "9 should be the letter" answer: 0 explain: "The cost depends on how many tickets there are. Let n be the number of tickets, then the cost is 9n." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#pia" text: "Pia writes the cost of $a$ apples at 3 dollars each. Click the line where her thinking goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: letter-as-object explain: "Line 2: 3a means 3 × a: 3 dollars times the number of apples. It does not mean \"3 apples\". The letter a stands for how many apples, a number." ``` ### A hall Here is how to build an expression for a situation. ```worked \text{Hall: 60 dollars, plus 5 dollars per guest} :: A hall costs 60 dollars to hire, and then 5 dollars for each guest. \text{Let } g = \text{number of guests} :: Say what the letter stands for. The number of guests changes, so $g$ stands for that. 5g :: Each guest costs 5 dollars, so $g$ guests cost $5 \times g$. 5g + 60 :: Add the hire, which is paid once. g = 10: \; 5(10) + 60 = 110 :: Test with a case you can check in words: 10 guests cost 50 + 60 = 110 dollars. g = 40: \; 5(40) + 60 = 260 :: Now the same expression gives any case, with no counting. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Pia's working one line at a time. What does the letter $a$ stand for? ### Your turn Say what the letter stands for first. Then build the expression. ## Modify: new situations ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a fee plus a rate, a quantity that goes down, two letters, and using the expression for a big case." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#taxi", height: 420 } tasks: - starter: "formula.yml#taxi" check: type: answer q: "A taxi costs 3 dollars to get in plus 2 dollars per km. Let $d$ be the number of km. Write an expression for the fare." answer: "2d + 3" feedback: - ["3d + 2", "The 3 dollars is paid once, to get in. Which amount is paid for each km?"] explain: "2d + 3. Check with d = 4: 8 + 3 = 11 dollars." - starter: "formula.yml#tank" check: type: answer q: "A tank holds 100 litres and loses 4 litres each minute. Let $m$ be the minutes. Write an expression for the litres left." answer: "100 - 4m" feedback: - ["100 + 4m", "The tank is losing water, so take 4m away."] - ["4m - 100", "Start from the 100 litres you have and take away what has gone: 100 − 4m."] explain: "100 − 4m: it starts at 100 and 4 litres go each minute. Check with m = 5: 100 − 20 = 80." - starter: "formula.yml#tickets" check: type: answer q: "Adult tickets cost 8 dollars and child tickets cost 5 dollars. Let $a$ be the number of adults and $c$ the number of children. Write an expression for the total cost." answer: "8a + 5c" feedback: - ["13ac", "Adults and children cost different amounts. Work out each group, then add them."] - ["8c + 5a", "Check which price goes with which group: adults cost 8 dollars."] explain: "8a + 5c: 8 dollars for each of a adults, plus 5 dollars for each of c children." - starter: "formula.yml#use" check: type: answer q: "Tickets cost $T = 12n + 6$ dollars for $n$ tickets (6 dollars booking). Use the expression to find the cost of 50 tickets." answer: "606" feedback: - ["56", "Put n = 50 in: 12 × 50, then add the 6 dollar booking."] - ["600", "Don't forget the 6 dollar booking fee."] explain: "12 × 50 + 6 = 600 + 6 = 606 dollars." ``` ### A taxi The board follows the situation and shows the result. Write your expression, then check it with a number. ### A tank ### Two groups ### A big case ## Practise: build and use ```step stage: practise insight: "Naming the letter, building the expression and using it for a larger case, mixed; the review is brackets." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A plumber charges 60 dollars call-out plus 40 dollars per hour. Let $h$ be the number of hours. Write an expression for the cost." answer: "40h + 60" feedback: - ["60h + 40", "The call-out fee is paid once. The 40 dollars is paid for each hour."] explain: "40h + 60: 40 dollars for each hour, plus 60 dollars once." - check: type: answer q: "Using $40h + 60$, what does a job of 3.5 hours cost, in dollars?" answer: "200" feedback: - ["350", "That multiplies 40 + 60 by 3.5. The 60 is paid once, so only 40 is multiplied."] explain: "40 × 3.5 + 60 = 140 + 60 = 200 dollars." - check: type: question q: "Cupcakes cost 3 dollars each. What should the letter $c$ stand for in the expression $3c$ for the total cost?" options: ["The number of cupcakes", "Cupcakes", "The cost"] answer: 0 explain: "c is a number: how many cupcakes. 3c is then 3 dollars times that number." - check: type: answer q: "Review: find $3(n + 4)$ when $n = 5$." answer: "27" feedback: - ["19", "That is 3 × 5 + 4. Do the brackets first: 5 + 4, then × 3."] explain: "3 × (5 + 4) = 3 × 9 = 27." - check: type: answer q: "Review: write an expression for \"add 5 to $n$, then multiply the result by 2\"." answer: "2(n + 5)" feedback: - ["2n + 5", "That doubles only n. The 2 multiplies the whole n + 5: use brackets."] explain: "2(n + 5): add 5 first, then double the whole result." ``` ### A plumber ### Using it ### The letter ### Review one ### Review two ## Make: a situation of your own ```step stage: make insight: "Inventing a situation and its expression reverses the lesson: from an expression back to a story." check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote what my letter stands for, wrote an expression for my own situation, and tested it with a number I could check in words." } ``` Make up a situation with a fee paid once and a price for each one: a club, a game, a delivery. Write "Let ___ be the number of ___." Then write an expression for the total, and test it with one case. Stretch: swap with a partner and see if they can write your expression from the story alone. ## Make: a fence, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A fence of p panels needs p + 1 posts, not 2p: the posts between panels are shared. Testing the expression on a fence small enough to draw shows which one it is, and then 18 panels needs no drawing." hint: ["Draw 3 panels in a row and count the posts.", "Every panel adds one post, and the first post is extra."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A straight fence has a post at each end and a post between every two panels. The club's fence will be 18 panels long (made up for the task). Let $p$ be the number of panels. Write an expression for the number of posts, then use it to find how many posts to order." steps: - ["Let $p$ be the number of panels", "the letter stands for the number that changes"] - ["3 panels need 4 posts when I draw them, so posts $= p + 1$", "test the expression on a case I can count"] - ["$18 + 1 = 19$ posts", "put $p = 18$ into the expression"] - ["Check another way: 18 panels have a post at their right-hand end, and there is one more post at the very start", "$18 + 1 = 19$ again"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why is the number of posts $p + 1$ and not $2p$?" options: - "Neighbouring panels share a post, and the first post is extra" - "Every panel has two posts of its own" - "A fence of $p$ panels needs $p$ posts" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Draw it: the post between two panels belongs to both, so it is only counted once.", "Draw 3 panels. The last panel needs a post at its far end too, so that is 4 posts."] answer: "19" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["36", "That is $2 \\times 18$. Neighbouring panels share a post."] - ["18", "That is one post for each panel. The first panel needs a post at both of its ends."] criteria: - "I said what $p$ stands for." - "I tested my expression on a fence I drew and counted (3 panels, 4 posts)." - "My answer for 18 panels is one more than 18." explain: "posts $= p + 1$, so 18 panels need $18 + 1 = 19$ posts. A real fence with corners or a gate needs more." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The 18 panels are made up for the task, and the fence is straight: corners and gates each add a post. Draw a few panels first, say what the letter stands for, then write the expression and type the number of posts. **Also used in** - **Fences and decking.** Posts, rails and boards are ordered from a rule like $p + 1$, without drawing the whole job. - **Chairs and tables.** Joined tables seat a number that follows a rule in the number of tables, so one expression covers any size. - **Next lessons.** Growing patterns and tables: the same kind of rule, shown in a table and then on a graph. ```teacher summary: Students say what a letter stands for, write an expression for a situation with a fee and a rate, test it with a case they can check, and use it for any number (AC9M7A02, node 3). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min struggle: Saying what the letter stands for before writing anything. Many students want the letter to be the answer, the total cost. Ask for the sentence "Let ___ be the number of ___" first, every time. goals: - I can say what the letter in an expression stands for, a number that changes. - I can write an expression for a situation with a once-only amount and an amount for each one. - I can test my expression with a case I can check in words, then use it for a big case. before: > Do the Modify boards yourself first. The mystery boards follow the situation, so students check their expression against them before they answer. The new move is saying what the letter stands for before writing anything. Two common errors: letting the letter be the thing worked out ("Let n be the cost"), and reading the letter as the object (Pia's mistake: 3a means 3 apples). Insist on the sentence "Let ___ be the number of ___". The once-only amount is a constant added on; the amount for each one is multiplied by the letter. This is the same structure as y = mx + c in Linear relations, so say so, but do not name it yet. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Ask a student who chose 'the total cost' what n would be for a trip of 30 students." - "Run: before moving n, ask what the cost is for 0 students. What does the 50 mean?" - "Investigate: model the worked example live. Write 'Let g be...' first, every time." - "Modify: ask for the sentence 'Let ___ be the number of ___' before each expression." - "Practise: for the plumber questions, ask which amount is paid once." - "Make: have students swap situations and write each other's expressions." - "Paper: the fence task is worked in books; the page marks the number of posts (19) and the reason for p + 1. Books out, and look for a drawn fence with the posts counted before any expression appears." stuck: - see: "A student reads a letter as an object (Pia's mistake: 3a means 3 apples)." ask: If a is 5, what is 3a? Is it 3 apples or something else? fix: a stands for a number, how many apples. 3a is 3 dollars times that number. - see: A student multiplies the once-only amount (60h + 40 for a 60 dollar call-out). ask: Does the call-out change if the job is 1 hour or 10 hours? fix: An amount paid once is added on. Only the price for each hour is multiplied by h. stretch: A shop sells pens at 2 dollars each and rulers at 3 dollars each, with a 1 dollar bag. Let p be pens and r rulers. Write the cost, then find it for 10 pens and 4 rulers. support: "Give a sentence frame: Let ___ be the number of ___. Paid once: ___. For each: ___. Expression: ___." leads: > This finishes the Expressions unit. The Equations unit starts from expressions like these: what number of students makes the trip cost 290? In Linear relations the same structure becomes y = mx + c and its graph. exit: q: A gym costs 30 dollars to join plus 15 dollars a week. Write what your letter stands for, an expression for the total, and the cost after 8 weeks. a: "Let w be the number of weeks. Total = 15w + 30. After 8 weeks: 15 × 8 + 30 = 150 dollars." explain: > To write an expression for a situation: (1) say **what the letter stands for**: the number that changes, such as the number of guests; (2) multiply it by the amount for each one; (3) add anything paid only once. A hall costing 60 dollars plus 5 dollars per guest, with $g$ guests, is $5g + 60$. Test the expression with one case you can check in words, then use it for any number. The letter stands for a number, not for the objects: in $3a$, $a$ is how many apples. ```
files.formula.yml:
# Boards for "An expression for any case". The run and use boards show the formula; the check boards are mystery
# rules (hide: formula) that students compare their expression with.

# region: run
widget: formula
formula: C = 12n + 50
slider n: 0, 40, 5
units: dollars
# endregion

# region: taxi
widget: formula
formula: T = 2d + 3
hide: formula
slider d: 0, 20, 4
# endregion

# region: tank
widget: formula
formula: L = 100 - 4m
hide: formula
slider m: 0, 25, 5
# endregion

# region: tickets
widget: formula
formula: T = 8a + 5c
hide: formula
slider a: 0, 10, 2
slider c: 0, 10, 3
# endregion

# region: use
widget: formula
formula: T = 12n + 6
slider n: 0, 60, 5
# endregion

# region: pic
widget: formula
formula: C = 5g + 60
slider g: 0, 40, 10
units: dollars
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: formula
formula: C = 5g + 60
slider g: 0, 40, 10, 10
units: dollars
# endregion
